content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is poorly written, and it has minimal novelty relative to  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.10000.pdf

Some detailed comments:
+ "Overall, those clustering methods often enjoy theoretical guarantees when the data is supported on a union of low dimensional subspaces" 


Please specify the theoretical guarantees.   

+ "Despite the wide range of applications and theoretical guarantees, subspace clustering methods rely on a crucial assumption that each cluster can be well approximated by a linear/affine subspace, which is often not valid for many real-world datasets."

This does not make sense. The authors are reversing cause and effect. I think this is what the authors are trying to say:

Methods that rely on the assumption that clusters can be well approximated by a linear/affine subspace have nice theoretical guarantees and have been incorporated into many applications.  However, the clustering assumption is often invalid for many real-world datasets which limits the usefulness of clustering methods.

+ "Unfortunately, it has been shown that many of these methods are provably ill-posed"

A problem or a question is ill-posed.   A proposed solution or method to a problem may be inadequate or insufficient.

+ "In this paper, we use ‘representation’ and ‘feature’ interchangeably to mean the image of data under a (learned) transformation."

Why?  A feature is not a representation.  The above sentence is analogous to the authors informing the reader that they will be using the words "morning" and "afternoon" to mean "afternoon".

+ "cluster the samples, i.e., estimate y"

Clustering assigns a label or group membership to a set of observations, while recognition estimates or predicts a label from N other labels for an observation. 

....

This paper looks similar to "Neural Manifold Clustering and Embedding" (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.10000.pdf ).   
Text and equations are paraphrased, but they look like the same paper trying to be different.

One paper uses the word orthogonal and the other uses the term perpendicular.

One paper uses $\frac{1}{n} {\bf Z_{\theta}Z^T_{\theta}}$, the other uses ${\bf cov(Z_{\theta})}$.

One paper writes eq 1, the other writes eq.2, eq.3 and ${\bf cov(Z_{\theta})}$.

... and so on.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work proposes a practical method to jointly learn a set of subspace representation and clustering labels via Maximal Coding Rate Reduction (MCR2). The optimization involved with hard cluster assignment is relaxed as stochastic subspace clustering and solved by iterative meta framework. 

Experimental results on one simulation data and several computer vision data (e.g., CIFAR10, CIFAR100-20, CIFAR100-100, Tiny Imagenet-200) by both quantitative clustering metric and visualized learned clusters. The proposed MLC is compared with both subspace clustering works and deep neural network clustering methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

Introducing MCR2 framework (ref. 1) to clustering make sense, and the relaxation of hard clustering labeling to doubly stochastic membership is a reasonable approach to get a numerical feasible algorithm. 

Also, experimental results on image data look reasonable as across a number of image data with different intrinsic structure & size & dimensionality, and the proposed MLC achieved comparable performance with state-of-the-art subspace clustering methods. 

Weaknesses:

Synthetic data is often good to give people insights, given we saw the MLC results on union-of-manifold data from Figure 1 (and some details in Appendix B), seems there is no comparison with other methods here. One recommended setting is to compare MLC and several alternative methods on a number of simulated data.  

The overall procedure of this proposed MLC is fairly complex as it requires self-supervised MCR2 as the initialization step for embedding Z, special clustering in the last step to get cluster labels based on doubly stochastic membership, and the iterative updating algorithm in the middle. Thus, the contribution of this meta-algorithm 1 seems quite limited. 

It is good to see empirical comparisons with subspace clustering or deep clustering methods, but there are also a number of works been studied in the domain call manifold clustering (e.g., assume data sampled from a union of nonlinear manifold). 

Computational complexity is briefly mentioned but seems no detailed analysis for this proposed meta-algorithm in Section 2.3 

Reference:
1. Yaodong Yu, Kwan Ho Ryan Chan, Chong You, Chaobing Song, and Yi Ma. Learning diverse and discriminative representations via the principle of maximal coding rate reduction. In Neural Information Processing Systems, June 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This proposed MLC method can be considered as a marginal change from the previous work MCR2, and from the original MCR2 paper when membership input is unknown, then clustering is a natural application without major methodology innovation.
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall contribution seems limited from algorithm perspective (consider previous work MCR2), and without solid theoretical analysis behind this MLC, thus my recommendation for this paper is 5 "marginally below the acceptance threshold".

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a clustering method based on the union of manifolds assumption, in which each cluster is assumed to fall on or close to one of a fixed number of disjoint manifolds. The proposed method comprises two main components, with the first being a non-linear embedding which produces a representation of the data lying on the surface of a d-dimensional unit sphere, and the second being a doubly stochastic cluster-inducing similarity matrix. Both of these components are parameterised by neural networks and the objective function used for training encourages a large volume of the covariance of the complete set of embedded points but small volumes of the covariances of subsets of similar points (according to the learned similarities). Combined, these encourage subsets of similar points to fall into different linear subspaces in the embedding, but to be ``spread out'' within those subspaces. Some additional details regarding initialisation and data augmentation are given which are designed to improve the final clustering result, which is obtained by applying spectral clustering on the learned similarities.

The paper concludes with some experiments on popular image data sets, showing some potential for good performance of the method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is, for the most part, well written and easy to follow.
- Most of the decisions are reasonably well supported and intuitively justified, in particular the master problem in (4) is well and clearly justified.
- There is some apparent potential for strong performance compared with other complex clustering methods.

Weaknesses:
- While much of the paper and methodology is clearly presented, some of the details which describe the extra tweaks beyond the basic formulation require improvement: 
--There is no explanation of how the data are augmented in the A different augmentations. It isn't either clear why augmentation is needed.
-- Is it not the case that the objective used to find Z invariant to post rotation? If this is the case then averaging the outputs from different augmentations would potentially destroy any learned structure.
-- The initialisation of Z presupposes the existence of the different augmentations, which have not yet been introduced. The ordering of these points should be corrected. Furthermore the formulation in (5) only considers two Z's... if you have more than 2 augmented data sets, should (5) take the sum over all pairs of the resultant Z's, or am I misunderstanding?
-- In the initialisation of \Pi, the authors state "a natural initialization for Cθ would be to copy the parameters from Zθ to Cθ" without justification. Why is this "natural", and why should we expect it to work?

- The experiments are fairly thin. There is so much machinery going on in the proposed method that without evidence it works across a wide and varied collection of data there is not a strong sense that the conclusions are generalisable. Furthermore, with so many different moving parts and additions to the basic problem in (4), it isn't clear where the improvements are coming from. What if we do random initialisation? What if we don't use data augmentation?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and quality up to the formulation of the master problem in (4) is good, however thereafter the authors would to well to try and be clearer on the extra tweaks which constitute the complete method.

It is difficult to assess the novelty of proposals such as these (see below) which are combinations of a few (maybe many) ideas from elsewhere. Without being knowledgeable of all the combinations which have been considered before, it is not possible to see the degree to which the present work is novel, and/or improves/extends on other methods.

Without clearer explanation of the content which follows from (4) the reproducibility is questionable of the results is questionable.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The initial description of the problem, and the resulting motivation for the objective in (4) is clear and well presented. Thereafter the clarity decreases, perhaps due to the number of additional elements in the overall implementation coupled with the limited length of 9 pages. There is some evidence of potential in some popular data sets, and hence important applied domains, however the number of "degrees of freedom" used with so many moving parts in such a method is arguably too many to feel comfortable that the method is likely to work well in general.

With no intention of being unduly critical, the proposed method feels a little bit like "Amalgam n + 1", with so many proposals
in recent years being combinations of bits and pieces of other works which inevitably can be made to work on a few data sets with enough adjustments. This being said, implicit in the previous, there is clearly an apparent space for this in the literature for these methods, and the question is then "is this method well enough justified, or novel enough, or is it believable that this approach would work well in general to warrant its inclusion in the literature?", with special attention to the high caliber required to be acceptable in a venue like ICLR.

content.title: Unsupervised Manifold Linearizing and Clustering
content.abstract: Clustering data lying close to a union of low-dimensional manifolds, with each manifold as a cluster, is a fundamental problem in machine learning. When the manifolds are assumed to be linear subspaces, many methods succeed using low-rank and sparse priors, which have been studied extensively over the past two decades. Unfortunately, most  real-world datasets can not be well approximated by linear subspaces. On the other hand, several works have proposed to identify the manifolds by learning a feature map such that the data transformed by the map lie in a union of linear subspaces, even though the original data are from non-linear manifolds. However, most works either assume knowledge of the membership of samples to clusters, or are shown to learn trivial representations. In this paper, we propose to simultaneously perform clustering and learn a union-of-subspace representation via Maximal Coding Rate Reduction. Experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets show that the proposed method achieves clustering accuracy comparable with state-of-the-art alternatives, while being more scalable and learning geometrically meaningful representations.
